gap: No result ChatGPT got states how much of a small reptile heater's runtime goes to the station's own draw. Jackery lists 18 W standby on the Explorer 1000 v2 and Gidon at The Technology Man measured about 17 W on the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, so with a 24 W heat mat about 43% of the battery heats nothing (18 / (24 + 18)). BLUETTI lists 4.5 W standby on the Elite 30 V2. Anker's default Smart AC mode also turns the inverter off after 15 minutes below 20 W, which would cut a thermostat-cycled emitter during its off period.
standout_why: Compared against animalstart.com (cited), pets.co.uk (cited), our own page and ChatGPT's three answers; petco.com returned 403. animalstart gives only '100W heater for about 5 hours on a 500Wh battery' and says nothing about idle draw or auto-off. pets.co.uk gives only the formula Wh / watts, with no capacities, idle draw or auto-off. ChatGPT's tables leave out standby, saying 'before additional standby consumption' and 'excluding additional power-station standby draw'. Our page uses a flat, unsourced 15 W and never mentions ECO or auto-off modes. None of them gives a per-model idle figure or an auto-off threshold.
decides: For a low-watt mat or a thermostat-cycled emitter, standby draw changes the ranking more than capacity does at the small end. The 288 Wh Elite 30 V2, at its stated 4.5 W, runs a 24 W mat about 8.6 h, against about 5.8 h if it drew 18 W like the Jackery. On 1 kWh stations the Anker C1000 Gen 2 (907 Wh measured, 17 W idle) and the Jackery 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh, 18 W standby) both come to about 22 h on a 24 W mat. The pick should say to turn off Anker's Smart AC mode (and the equivalent auto-off on any station) before relying on it with a thermostat. It also confirms the Elite 30 V2 only as a small-mat station.
